---
title: "Quasi-Poisson regression"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Quasi-Poisson regression keeps the Poisson mean function but allows the scaled
[variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#variance-as-expected-squared-distance),
the expected squared distance from the conditional mean, stated below.

Unlike a [PMF](../random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions.qmd), the quasi specification supplies a mean--variance relation without a complete response distribution. [Covariance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) still matters when rows share unmodeled regional information. A **random effect** is provisionally a shared group deviation; the [fixed-and-random-effects page](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) develops it as a population model.

If the fitted mean equation is retained while its Poisson variance is relaxed,
the coefficient estimates stay put and their uncertainty changes. The response
remains the reported geopolitical total defined in the [country-language
measurement dossier](poisson-regression.qmd#nettle-country-language-measurement);
changing its variance model leaves cross-border overlap and documentation
differences in the measurement process.

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\phi\mu_i.
$$

It thus changes uncertainty, not fitted means. The Nettle data show the distinction directly.

For a mean model $\mu_i(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and variance function $V(\mu_i)=\mu_i$, the quasi-score is

$$
\mathbf U_Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
=
\sum_i
\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\phi\mu_i}
\frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}.
$$

With the log link, $\partial\mu_i/\partial\boldsymbol\beta=\mu_i\mathbf x_i$, so

$$
\mathbf U_Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
=
\frac{1}{\phi}
\sum_i\mathbf x_i(y_i-\mu_i).
$$

The Poisson score is the same sum without the constant $1/\phi$. Multiplying a score by a nonzero constant does not change its root. This is why the Poisson and quasi-Poisson coefficient estimates agree for the same mean specification.

```{r}
#| label: load-and-fit-quasi
#| echo: true
path <- "data/nettle/nettle-1999-climate.csv"
if (file.exists(path)) {
  nettle <- read.csv(path)
} else {
  url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/",
                "applied_statistics_book_data/master/nettle_1999_climate.csv")
  source_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  download.file(url, source_file, mode = "wb")
  stopifnot(digest::digest(source_file, "sha256", file = TRUE, serialize = FALSE) ==
    "3c5abfbec7b2132a9b81ee9a178cbd5559426578032b60c6c4ad74046898793b")
  raw <- read.csv(source_file)
  nettle <- data.frame(country = raw$Country, log10_population = raw$Population,
    log10_area_km2 = raw$Area, log_area_km2 = log(10) * raw$Area,
    mean_growing_season_months = raw$MGS, language_count = as.integer(raw$Langs))
}
formula <- language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + offset(log_area_km2)
poisson_fit <- glm(formula, poisson(), nettle)
quasi_fit <- glm(formula, quasipoisson(), nettle)
stopifnot(max(abs(fitted(poisson_fit) - fitted(quasi_fit))) < 1e-8)
data.frame(
  model = c("Poisson", "quasi-Poisson"),
  mgs_estimate = c(coef(poisson_fit)[[2L]], coef(quasi_fit)[[2L]]),
  mgs_standard_error = c(summary(poisson_fit)$coefficients[2L, 2L],
                         summary(quasi_fit)$coefficients[2L, 2L]),
  dispersion = c(1, summary(quasi_fit)$dispersion)
)
```

The MGS coefficient and every fitted rate are identical, while the standard error expands from `r round(summary(poisson_fit)$coefficients[2L, 2L], 4)` to `r round(summary(quasi_fit)$coefficients[2L, 2L], 4)`. The estimated dispersion is `r round(summary(quasi_fit)$dispersion, 2)`.

The [covariance](../random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd#definition) estimate, which records joint coefficient uncertainty on the model scale, is multiplied by $\widehat\phi$, so each standard error is multiplied by $\sqrt{\widehat\phi}$. This connects the variance repair to the [standard-error definition](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd). The fitted mean does not move because the quasi-score root does not move.

```{r}
#| label: plot-quasi-shared-fit
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
nettle$rate <- nettle$language_count / exp(nettle$log_area_km2)
grid <- data.frame(mean_growing_season_months =
  seq(min(nettle$mean_growing_season_months),
      max(nettle$mean_growing_season_months), length.out = 200L))
grid$rate <- exp(coef(quasi_fit)[[1L]] + coef(quasi_fit)[[2L]] *
                   grid$mean_growing_season_months)
ggplot(nettle, aes(mean_growing_season_months, rate)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) + geom_line(data = grid, color = "#1F5A85", linewidth = .8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Mean growing season (months)", y = "Languages per square kilometer") +
  theme_classic()
```

Quasi-likelihood does not define a complete [probability mass function](../random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions.qmd), which would assign normalized probabilities across every possible count, so ordinary likelihood comparisons such as [AIC](../model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd) are unavailable. AIC ranks a specified candidate set using maximized likelihood plus a parameter penalty; it is not a model-adequacy test. Quasi-Poisson instead enlarges the variance used for standard errors. The mean still treats area as proportional exposure, and the rows still aggregate languages, documentation practices, and shared histories within country boundaries.

| Repair | Mean structure | Variance or dependence | Full likelihood? |
|---|---|---|---|
| revise predictors/link | changes | implied by chosen family | yes, if a family is specified |
| quasi-Poisson | same Poisson mean | $\phi\mu$ | no |
| negative binomial | may be the same | $\mu+\mu^2/\theta$ | yes |
| random effects | conditional mean gains group terms | induces marginal dispersion and dependence | yes |

In the last row, a **random effect** is a group-specific deviation represented as
a draw from a shared distribution; [fixed and random effects](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd)
develops that construction later. A large dispersion estimate alone does not
identify a grouping factor or license such a term.

Thus quasi-Poisson is useful when the mean equation is the target and a proportional variance relation is defensible. It rescales coefficient covariance under that declared relation. Because the specification supplies no normalized probability across possible counts, it cannot assign count probabilities or identify which linguistic, geographic, or documentation process produced the extra variation.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why do Poisson and quasi-Poisson coefficients agree here?
2. By what factor do quasi-Poisson standard errors change?
3. Why is ordinary AIC unavailable?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Their score equations differ only by the constant $1/\phi$, so they have the same root for a fixed mean model. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. Covariances are multiplied by $\widehat\phi$ and standard errors by $\sqrt{\widehat\phi}$. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. AIC requires a maximized probability likelihood, while quasi-Poisson specifies mean and variance without a complete PMF. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>
